speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to raise a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. The town of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, was settled in 1753 by immigrants from the Palati-nate-Wurtemberg and other states in the region, Montbe-liard and Switzerland. This year the town and its citizens celebrate their two hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary. Since the initial celebrations of this event begin next week, I move, seconded by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald):
That congratulations and best wishes be extended by this House to the mayor, council and citizens of one of the first real Canadian settlements under British auspices for the significant contribution made by its citizens to the history and economic development of our nation over the past two and one-quarter centuries, as illustrated by the schooner Bluenose on the Canadian ten-cent piece.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
That this House deeply regrets that the government, through neglect or because of its connivance with the police, allowed the whole of Canada in general and Quebec in particular to be engulfed in a crisis such as the one we experienced in October 1970, and therefore directs the Solicitor General to disclose in public all the facts and circumstances pertaining to the authority

February 17, 1978

given to the RCMP to act as they did before, during and after the October 1970 events.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in order to put this motion in its context and fully understand the purpose of its presentation today, one must remember that, one day in 1970, we woke up in a nightmare and we have not been able to determine as yet who was responsible for those events which not only traumatized the population of an entire nation but cast reflections on a particular province of this country which, in my opinion, represents a people and a nation as well. And we can say that never in its history this people and this nation have participated voluntarily in any conflict, even the one in 1755 which opposed both parent states and not those Canadians who were here at that time.
Mr. Speaker, when this nation had the opportunity in 1775 to join the American colonies in their rebellion, they chose not to do so. They were placed in similar circumstances in 1812, and more recently during the Boer War, World War I and World War II, but the people in Quebec have never accepted violence as a means of settling any conflicts and even less as a means of promoting its emancipation and development.
Mr. Speaker, such a people could not create the terrorist movement that led to the famous October 1970 crisis. We must therefore denounce those responsible in order to save the pride and dignity of the Quebec and the Canadian people. Our country should not have faced such a situation. Mr. Speaker, the serious suspicions we have about the federal government can be substantiated, and this is what I shall try to do while discussing this motion.
Before dealing more specifically with this motion I wish to conclude those preliminary remarks by referring to an incident that should be explained some day to prove that Quebecers are not really responsibile for the terrorism outburst that took place in our country in the sixties and reached its climax in 1970. The founder of the FLQ is one Georges Schoeters. He was neither a Quebecer nor a Canadian but an individual who came from Belgium and who, after visiting our country and Cuba, decided to start that movement. That man was also an ardent supporter of the British monarchy. At least he was during the First ten years he spent in this country. Now, the founder of the FLQ who was convicted in the early sixties for bomb attacks, that individual convicted for criminal offences is today at large in Belgium. I would like to know why the Canadian government agreed that this terrorist be released on parole and sent back to Belgium.
Why has the Belgium government agreed to admit a terrorist formally convicted of criminal offences here in Canada? Mr. Speaker, those questions regarding the circumstances surrounding the release and extradition of that Georges Schoeters, the FLQ founder, must be answered. Why has Belgium agreed to his repatriation since he had the Canadian citizenship? Mr. Speaker, this requires an explanation. But rather than make accusations, we should kick out of office those who are actually responsible for the chaotic situation we went

through. I would even go as far as to say. Mr. Speaker, that our present economic and financial difficulties might also be due partially to that confusion. That is why the motion specifically says "through neglect or because of its connivance".
Mr. Speaker, in 1970, more specifically on December 10 of that year, I had all the reasons in the world to inquire about the actual circumstances surrounding that famous crisis, that famous crisis which upset the whole country, that famous crisis which led to the adoption of war measures and put the Canadian armed forces on a war footing, that crisis when an insurrection was apprehended. It was even said at the time that the then editor of Le Devoir, Claude Ryan, headed a parallel government. He seems in fact to be accomplishing this now by running for the leadership of the Quebec Liberal party. On December 10, 1970, Mr. Speaker, I asked the government just how far the RCMP had infiltrated the FLQ. The reply was as follows, and I quote:
In answering his question, may I say that in accordance with long-established practice it is not in the public interest to reveal this type of information.
That was the reply given. I had every reason to demand to be told who exactly was Pierre Seguin, alias Yves Langlois, or the opposite, Yves Langlois, alias Pierre Seguin, of the cell responsible for kidnapping Mr. Cross. Who was this Seguin? What was his relation to the RCMP? I received no answer! I was told it was because of "State security". More recently, when little by little the former Solicitor General told us about certain somewhat irregular activities of the RCMP, I was told that if I had something to say, I should simply appear before the Macdonald Commission.
Mr. Speaker, if through neglect or its connivance with police authorities, this government contributed to the state of affairs which finally led to the October 1970 crisis, how can this same government, which appoints its friends to this commission, tell us the truth. How can we get at the truth if the terms of reference of this same commission repeat the answer that I was given on December 10, 1970? How can we have confidence in this commission if its terms of reference are:
to advise and make such report as the Commissioners deem necessary and desirable in the interest of Canada, regarding the policies and procedures governing the activities of the RCMP in the discharge of its responsibility to protect the security of Canada-
This reason is always invoked to keep something secret. But how can we know this? Mr. Speaker, we are faced with a situation ten times worse than the Watergate affair in the United States. If the truth came out in the United States, it is because American institutions allowed for proper scrutiny. But how can the suspects be at the same time the investigators and the judges? How can we discover the truth?
The terms of reference then say:
-adequacy of the laws of Canada as they apply to such policies and procedures, having regard to the needs of the security of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps everything was cooked up and that story of terrorism in Quebec was kept alive in order to cast reflections on honest Quebecers who wanted to promote the emancipation and the development of their country.

February 17, 1978

The War Measures Act was invoked under the pretence of national security and of a state of apprehended insurrection. Mr. Speaker, how many people were sentenced as a result of the October 1970 crisis? Ten. The whole army was put on alert, we were told there was a state of apprehended insurrection and yet only ten persons were actually involved in these FLQ cells. Still some 3,000 persons were harassed for all sorts of reasons. At one time even I feared I could be intimidated because in 1963, having been accused of terrorism, I had had the opportunity to learn a little about the methods of the police. That story made headlines in Quebec newspapers in 1963.
At that time I had learned quite a few things and this is why today, I can speak knowledgeably about these events. Yet, Mr. Speaker, out of these 3,000 persons who were harassed and out of the 500 others who had a taste of what our jails are like, only ten had done things for which accusations could be laid against them. However, I repeat, we have recently discovered that the RCMP allowed itself to commit burglaries, something which has been admitted by the Solicitor General and the government itself. It has also been discovered that the RCMP allowed itself, always according to that special committee, to set criminal fires. It has been candidly revealed to us that the RCMP took the liberty of stealing dynamite! Mr. Speaker, let me elaborate on that: what was the purpose of stealing that dynamite? If the authorities needed dynamite, they only had to get the necessary permit to buy it; why steal it? Mr. Speaker, how many times has this been done during and before the October 70 crisis? The former minister called me irresponsible because I voiced my suspicions about the procedural methods of the RCMP and even sometime alleging that some individuals might have been liquidated, before making any inquiry about it. Right then he said I was irresponsible. He had himself said that there had been no such event before 1972 and 1973 the year the break-in took place. Now, on January 9, once again the Solicitor General very candidly confessed that in 1971 the Royal Canadian Mounted Police took upon itself to issue a communique in the name of the FLQ which invited the population to commit acts of violence and insurrection. Mr. Speaker, this is just too much. Soon the inquiry will bear on things which happened in 1970. The inquiry has now gone back to 1971 and soon it will study 1970. That is why the Solicitor General should ask himself the following questions and above all answer them: When did the RCMP start closely monitoring the activities of separatists, FLQ sympathizers, independentists and so on? At the instigation of which authority and which representatives of that authority did it undertake to infiltrate these movements? How were the results reported to the authorities?
Is it possible to know all orders or counter orders that have been given or received at the higher level since 1960 concerning any criminal activity the RCMP was responsible for monitoring, preventing or uncovering, particularly in the area of separatist activities that were viewed as illegal by the federal government? What was done after evidence was

received from the City of Montreal authorities in 1969? Mr. Speaker, we have a federal police with a tremendous reputation. And when the minister announced, barely 15 days ago, that the RCMP had succeeded in breaking a Soviet spy ring, I was as proud of our national police as everyone else. They are competent, I am even told they are one of the most competent police forces in the world. How come such a competent police force, capable of competing with Russian spies, could not uncover and arrest terrorists from 1962 to 1970?
Mr. Speaker, this issue is extremely serious. The force's reputation is at stake, and I could not be satisfied with the answer that what happens in Quebec does not concern the RCMP. We have ample proof that the RCMP were aware of terrorist activities as early as 1960, 1961, 1962, 1963. Mr. Speaker, when the former solicitor general responded to my allegations concerning Michel Viger, he simply dismissed this as idle talk. Mr. Speaker, I received a letter dated December 14, 1977 from Mr. Jean Viger, Michel Viger's brother, which was indeed published by the newspaper Le Devoir. I would like to quote from it the following paragraph pointing to questions for which we will need answers. I quote:
I must say the circumstances surrounding the death of my brother Michel, on my St. Nazaire farm in the summer of 1975, while mowing hay, are particularly disquieting. On that day I had gone to Longueuil. Michel was alone on my farm. When I came back his family was worried because he had not come to supper. Also worrying, I went directly to that part of the farm that remained to be mowed. There I saw the tractor but not my brother; but then I saw him motionless, lying on his belly under the humming tractor, his arm crushed under the weight, his left leg caught to the break pedals, his neck broken under the pressure of one of the tractor's back wheels. There was no tightness, no trace of struggling or pain. He had died instantly, and many hours before.
Oddly enough, the tractor was in neutral, oddly enough Michel was lying under his tractor, he who was so prudent with those machines, oddly enough that had happened right when I was absent, shortly after a series of filmed interviews with Louis Martin, a very small part of which was to appear on the program "Format 60" in the fall of 1975. So, Mr. Matte, I am inclined to believe as you do that Michel Viger was murdered by the CIA, the RCMP or people like that.
Mr. Speaker, those are very serious things I am saying but their seriousness must not stop us from finding out the truth so justice will be done.

When the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his gaggle of inferior ministers slunk out of the national confer-

ence with its collective tail between its legs, having suffered a very disastrous three days at the conference, the reasons were most obvious. One of the reasons was because of issues relating to what the hon. member has said in his motion and in his statements. The people of this country have lost confidence in the government because of its failure to tell the truth and because of its continued disposition to exaggerate, to conceal, and to fail to come forward and tell parliament and the public the facts behind so many of the issues of the day. That has become so obvious that the fog of suspicion, doubt, and disbelief which originates from Ottawa has spread over Canada.
No matter how valid its suggestions, when the government attempts to introduce programs regarding economic and social problems, it faces the insuperable obstacle that people no longer believe in it. Perhaps some of the ideas kicked around the conference were all right, but Canadians reject the statements made by the government and its ministers. When that occurs, the government cannot govern any more. In the type of complex world we live in, there must be a reasonable relationship of trust between the government and the people.
Another reason for the failure of the conference was the Quebec situation and much of the difficulties which exist regarding the question of national unity. Many of these questions in regard to national unity were initiated because of the events in October, 1970.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House recessed at one o'clock I think I had demonstrated to the satisfaction of most reasonable members that one of the main reasons for the failure of the recent economic conference, and the fact of the Prime Minister and his federal ministers crawling from it in a beaten and disspirited way, could be tied to this motion we have been discussing. I talked about the obsession for secrecy and furtiveness which has turned off most reasonable people in Canada with the result that no longer has this government any credibility; nor will it have credibility at any time, and the sooner it meets its fate at the polls the better for everybody.
The other reason for the failure of the conference is also referred to in this motion, and that is the problem which exists in Confederation because of a movement in the province of Quebec. I do not suggest for one minute that the government has to bear sole responsibility, but it has some responsibility for the situation which exists and which resulted in the failure
February 17, 1978

of that conference. This all stems from the situation and the facts that existed in 1970, 1972 and 1973.
I was here in 1970 and listened to the debates. I was House leader for this party and participated in some of those discussions. To recall the events and refresh one's memory one has only to read what was said by the then minister of regional economic expansion, now a Senator in the other place, but then the hon. member for Langelier. He made a very inflammatory and colourful speech. On October 16, 1970, he talked about several thousand active members of a group and indicated that probably some were armed.
He went on to say:
One thing is certain, Mr. Speaker-I don't know any more than the police, probably much less-there is an organization which has thousands of guns, rifles, machine guns, bombs and about 2,000 pounds of dynamite,-
It is interesting to recall in that context that one of the statements made by the security force was that they had stolen dynamite. It was put in the possession of FLQ so that it could be used as a means of trying to invoke action against them.
The minister went on to say:
-more than enough to blow up the core of downtown Montreal.
Then there was a book written later by the then secretary of state, now the distinguished ambassador to France, Mr. Pelletier, in which he referred, somewhat disparagingly, to the role of the Mounted Police in this issue and the facts leading up to the issue, a book which should be required reading for many of the current members of the House.
But what were the facts? Very simply what happened was that the War Measures Act was invoked. There was the tragic assassination of Mr. Laporte, and the subsequent state funeral manipulated on behalf of the government, as I understand it against the wishes of members of the family, so that it could be made into a media event. Then, because of the wishes of the then government of Quebec-and I think it only fair to say, a government which had been following the characteristic practices of the senior government in Ottawa, being secretive and arrogant and with elements of corruption, certainly a government which did not find favour with the people of Quebec-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: That is not for you to decide.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
The people of Quebec decided that, and that was one of the reasons for its defeat. I am a Canadian and I travel and talk to the people of Quebec, and many people in Quebec said to me that that was one of the main factors in the defeat of the Bourassa government-it was too much like the Trudeau government.
What happened after that was that there was some resist-ence to the act called the War Measures Act being used in time of peace and they decided very wisely, following requests of members of the House and of the province of Quebec, to bring in a substitute temporary measure, a Public Orders Act. As the then House leader I remember participating in arrangements by which it was agreed we would facilitate the passage

of the second act and would approve the motion introduced by the Prime Minister, by which the House purported to accept the actions of the government, provided the other act was brought in. There was an understanding at the time that some permanent legislation would later be introduced, and certainly the then minister of justice, Mr. Turner, said that discussions were going on-this was at the time he introduced the Public Orders Act, a temporary act-and it was his intention that permanent legislation be introduced. I think that was very wise. I point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to members of the House that many of the problems which exist today would never have existed had the government followed through on its announced intention.
In the spring of 1971 the government set up a special joint committee of this parliament which was to be charged with the responsibility of dealing with all matter leading up to the need to have a law dealing with domestic difficulties which would be somewhat more moderate than the provisions of the War Measures Act, and would not contain the connotation that it was a measure in any way related to war or to apprehended warfare. The motion was first introduced for debate on May 13, 1971, and was debated. The justice critic of this party, the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), moved an amendment by which he asked the House to agree that this committee would have the right to examine the facts leading up to the crisis of 1970. Mr. Speaker found that particular amendment to be in order and, the minute that was done, you should have seen the government troops run for the doors.
The then minister of justice spoke on May 19 and he made it pretty plain that, in his mind a motion of that kind establishing a joint committee with that kind of amendment to it was not one which the government would find satisfactory. So they ran away from it. The motion died on the order paper during a session which, you may recall, Mr. Speaker, lasted from 1970 to 1972. It was never brought back, despite requests from members on this side of the House as well as from some members on the other side. I see the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) here. He has been one who has urged the passage of suitably phrased legislation to deal with law and order in a domestic situation which, had it been in place in 1972 and 1973, would not have led to the current situation in which we find it necessary to establish Royal commissions to inquire into these problems. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont made a speech on October 27 of last year in which he called attention to this issue. As reported at page 344 of Hansard of that day he said:
It is important that despite the commitment made by the government leader in the House on October 27, 1975, a bill designed for such situations has not yet been introduced and the government has made no mention of it in its inaugural message.
It is interesting that the next day the Prime Minister was having a press conference at which someone picked up the statement of the hon. member, referred to it, and asked the Prime Minister what he said. The Prime Minister, with what I will call polite sophistry but which was in fact complete deception, said:
2982

February 17, 1978

Listen, I have no serious objections. In the months following the adoption of the War Measures Act by the government of which I was leader, I even expressed a desire to see this act replaced by provisions, probably added to the Criminal Code, which would enable us to act vigorously each time national security was threatened as it was in October 1970, without having to invoke the War Measures Act.
Then he went on to say that he did not bring it in because opposition members objected. That is an absolute falsehood. That was not the case. Nobody on this side of the House, and I believe I can speak for members of the NDP and the Creditist party when I say that no one from their parties, objected to it. We pressed continuously for the passage of such legislation, and if it had been in place in 1972 and 1973 this would have been a happier country. These scandals, these problems with various solicitors general, and the three inquiries would not have taken place as they did. But the Prime Minister had the unmitigated gall to say he did not do it because the opposition objected. When did this Prime Minister ever fail to take action which he thought he wanted to take because the opposition objected? That is absolute nonsense.
That brings us into what happened in 1972 and 1973. There is no doubt in my mind that the government knew-I do not say it initiated-in 1972 and 1973 what was going on then. I do not know who knew, but certainly people close enough to be part of the government apparatus were aware of what was going on. But they said nothing. The reason they said nothing in the fall of 1972 and 1973 was an issue of some bewilderment to me, until I happened to think about it.
What was the situation in the fall of 1972 and 1973? We had a minority government. What would have happened to the minority government had the Prime Minister disclosed publicly that security forces were engaged in these activities, and in particular had broken into the NDP offices? I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and his then leader, David Lewis, would have immediately dropped the government cold. They are honourable and respectable men. 1 disagree with them on most things, but on an issue of this kind there is no doubt at all about what would have been the facts and the minority government of the Prime Minister would have been defeated. That is why the government kept quiet about it. "What a tangled web we weave when first we practise to deceive." That is exactly what has developed since then.
However, I think that is the end of my comments about the government. We all know these are facts. We have to look together to what we can do to improve the government. This country will make progress only if we have in it government which is open, honest, and acceptable. 1 am not saying anything about a new government. That is beside the point. Sometimes we have to do more than change the players; we have to change the rules. This means the introduction of legislation. This party and other opposition parties are committed to open, honest, and acceptable government.
Before this government meets its fate I would like to see it adopt this principle and say that it stands for openness and honesty. That would do more than anything else I know of to

restore confidence in this country and a reasonable approach on the part of the people. It would do much to bring about a turn-around in our economic situation, which is essential if we are going to make progress. It is a challenge for this government and for the private members on the backbenches of the government side. Most of them believe in open government. Do they have enough courage to stand up to the Prime Minister and tell him that is what they want? If they do not, God help this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in rising to speak on opposition day for the second time since I was appointed to my present position, I did not expect I would be able to participate in the House debates, and I want to thank the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) for giving me this opportunity.
I paid particular attention to the remarks by the hon. member for Champlain, and from the way he worded his motion today I had hoped he would have somehow, suggested ways or means to help me discharge my duties as solicitor general responsible for national security in Canada. Unfortunately I did not hear such suggestions in his speech. Mr. Speaker, I am really sorry he did not because, he is fully aware that the question of national security is of prime importance and that we all like to dwell on that issue which is related, to the quality of life and freedom for Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) might like to comment on some of the remarks by the hon. member for Champlain, and I will ask him to do so. As for me, Mr. Speaker, I would rather limit my speech to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and national security.

I would like to make a few comments relating to the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), for whom I have great respect. That respect is in recognition of his ability to take advantage of the context of this House and what it provides, namely, an adversarial forum in which partisan interests come to the fore on a regular basis. I have yet to hear an advocate in the opposition who is better able to employ partisan argumentation and precise adversarial comments to carry out his responsibility. I know the hon. member has been around here for some time and has had a great deal of training in his trade in the opposition. He has not had much chance to sit on this side of the House. That is why he has become so competent in what he is doing.
I would like to call attention to the first point he made relating to a press release, a statement which was made by my counsel yesterday before the Keable inquiry, and the production of three documents which previously had been subject of an application under Section 41(2) by my predecessor.
If the hon. member had read the press release further, he would have seen that they were produced as a result of some confusion which had arisen and that had the circumstances of today been the circumstances when they were produced, those documents would not have been included within the affidavit
February 17, 1978

under Section 41(2). At the time my predecessor did not know of any illegal activity, and he did not have any knowledge of the "Ham" operation. It was all made clear by my predecessor. The hon. member is quite free to draw the partisan conclusions he has drawn. All I want him to do is recognize that there are additional comments which he did not draw to the attention of this Chamber to explain the circumstances surrounding the production of these documents.
I would like to deal with the matter of national security. The hon. member for Champlain has indicated in his motion that there is a crisis today which is similar to that of 1970. I listened to his comments, but I did not hear him indicate any events similar to the events of the late 1960's and the early 1970's. Where are the riots, bombs, and kidnappings we experienced at that time?
I am quite concerned about any indication that there could be a recurrence of the 1970 situation because one of my primary responsibilities is to avoid such a recurrence. I have been in my present portfolio for approximately two weeks. I have had a large number of briefings, and at my insistence there is an exchange of information on a regular basis. I am very well satisfied that the RCMP security service is an excellent service which discharges its responsibilities seriously.
I recognize that Canada, among all the countries with which we deal, is perhaps one of the most peaceful internally. It is one of the most inviolate in terms of external interference. It enjoys a very high reputation within the international community.
We have a large number of allies with which we exchange information on a regular basis. That exchange of information is a result of the confidence our allies have in our ability to preserve our own internal security and to protect our own national sovereignty. If there is one instrument which has been fundamental in securing that protection and reputation, it is the RCMP.
The RCMP is responsible for protecting us against subversive activities designed to undermine the confidence of Canadians and of our allies in our governments and institutions and designed to bring about governmental change by violence, force, terror or other criminal means. The RCMP is responsible for protecting us against the kind of trans-national terrorism experienced in less fortunate countries, a problem we do not have. I submit that the RCMP security service, by conscientiously doing its job, has protected Canadians from violence, from those who would weaken our NATO alliance and from those who would subvert our governments at all levels, as well as our institutions.
In October, 1970, action was taken by the government to establish the rule of law, a fundamental principle of our way of life, to ensure that the tragic events of that time did not occur again. It was clear that a proper intelligence on subversive activities was required. In gathering such intelligence certain unlawful acts were committed. I need not elaborate on those acts. They are now being considered by the inquiries set up by

the federal government and the provincial government of the province of Quebec, and the acts themselves have been referred to the attorneys general of the provinces involved. I am sure that you would agree that, in the total scheme of all RCMP activity, which is an ongoing process by a large force, there were very few unlawful acts and those were committed by very few people. I am not trying to condone them but simply to put the whole of the operations in perspective. We are dealing with acts that took place in the early 1970's, although we are now in 1978.

I would now like to address myself to the legal and constitutional aspects of our national security operations. As you know, many things have been written about the relations between the government and the Quebec Commission of inquiry chaired by Mr. Jean Keable which is considering some aspects of the RCMP activities in that province. When the PQ was elected in November 1976, the new Minister of Justice logically assumed the responsibilities of his predecessors with respect to the charges of allegedly illegal operations of the RCMP in Quebec. Mr. Bedard, in his own right, decided to set up a commission of inquiry chaired by Mr. Keable to shed light on the matter.
The federal government has recognized that commission and promised its full co-operation. However, some problems came up with the various redefinitions of the terms of reference granted to the Keable Commission and then the commissioner demanded the right to investigate, in my opinion, all RCMP operations. The federal did not and will not accept such terms of reference, as interpreted by the commissioner. It is also on the basis of that disagreement, that the question of legal responsibility in matters pertaining to national security of Canada has been raised.
I want to be clear on that point. All the allegedly illegal activities of the RCMP in Quebec known to the federal government have been brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice in that province, since he is responsible for the administration of justice in that province. Quebec has on hand all the facts of which I am aware and of which the RCMP is aware and if new facts were brought to the attention of the McDonald commission, they would also be referred to Quebec or any other province involved. Such is the procedure required under our constitution which we intend to follow.
If the Quebec Minister of Justice or the Attorney General of any province have sufficient grounds to delve any further into certain activities of the RCMP, it is their right to do so, but, Mr. Speaker, I think that a provincial Minister of Justice or Attorney General does not have the right to use such offences as a pretence to examine or inquire into all RCMP activities. The government as well as myself do insist on the difference between a possible illegal act committed by a member or a group of members of the RCMP and the regular ongoing activities of that police force, which is committed to protecting national security, and which is a federal body.
According to the government, this disrespect or unwillingness to admit this difference is the important factor in the
80031-47^2

February 17, 1978

debate which is presently going on between us and the Department of Justice of Quebec and the Keable Commission. The government has made its opinion known in court with respect not only to the way the Commission inquires into the alleged illegal acts committed by this police force, but also to the way they attempt to delve into all the activities of the RCMP. The RCMP is a federal agency and the federal government denies not only the government of Quebec, but also the government of any other province, the right to examine the day to day operations of that agency. One needs not draw before you, Mr. Speaker, the absurd parallel whereby the federal government would inquire into activities of a provincial government.
Mr. Speaker, if that principle is not upheld, any federal institution remains at the mercy of provincial governments. How could we expect Confederation to work in such circumstances? That is why, Mr. Speaker, the federal government has tried to have a restraining order issued against the Keable Commission. It was not, as it has stupidly been alleged by some people, because the then Solicitor General or the federal government want to evade justice or put a check on the PQ through the Keable Commission.
As a matter of fact, the Keable Commission and the PQ government want to do a detailed examination of all legal and illegal operations of the RCMP in Quebec. We do not intend to let them do it, Mr. Speaker. In the course of this debate, we are also aware of a confrontation between federal and provincial responsibilities in matters relating to national security in Canada. The Canadian government believes that he has the responsibility to safeguard national security in Canada against any threat whether from the inside or from the outside. Spying activities in Canada are part of the foreign policy of some countries and are closely linked with their perception of their own political, military, economic and cultural interests. Such is the case in Canada. Consequently, they must be seen in the Canadian national context and stopped by federal agencies which have jurisdiction under the Constitution on matters involving foreign countries and Canadian Defence.
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel it is possible to share with the provinces a responsibility which is totally within federal jurisdiction, pursuant to Section 91 of the Canadian Constitution. The same thing may be said about international and home bred terrorists who have given their all grance to foreign and international ideologies and who, judging from their outlook at least, are part of a terrorist conspiracy. Mr. Speaker, I cannot even imagine a situation where each province would claim the right to deal as it pleases either with the KGB or the Japanese Red Army or any other terrorist organization.
It may well be that the areas of responsibilities on matters involving national security are not well defined on account of the changes which have been taking place recently in Canada as far as police operations are concerned. In many respects, we and our allies are operating differently, as in a number of them there are major structural differences between law enforcing agencies and such groups which are responsible for national security.
Historically, in Canada, both those responsibilities have been assumed by the RCMP. It will doubtless be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry on Security, to which the hon. member for Perth-Wil-mot (Mr. Jarvis) made reference this morning, recommended the setting up of a security service separate and distinct from the RCMP. At that time, the government did not share that opinion but, following the report of the McDonald Commission, a similar recommendation may be made again. If such is the case, the government could reconsider it.
Mr. Speaker, one can certainly find arguments in support of both these previously denounced with regard to the security services. What must be remembered however, is that the federal government is responsible for ensuring the best possible mechanism to safeguard Canadian security against all foreign threats and most domestic dangers. In that regard, I want to stress that those threats to Canada are real, as we found out last week; because of them, Canada cannot do without a national security agency, and the one now responsible, though grappling with the problems now afflicting it, has done remarkably well, for the sake of our country, as I said before. Hundreds of foreign agents are operating in Canada in the intelligence field. Terrorists have entered Canada and others try to do so constantly. It is mostly thanks to the conscientious work performed by the Canadian groups in charge of security that our country has been unscathed by international events.
Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, the days of the Olympic Games in Montreal, when we were scared stiff that the events that took place in Germany during their own games might happen again. Thanks to the efforts and industry of the RCMP, there was no trouble, Mr. Speaker. I wonder if the people who organize such games would be willing to entrust to the provinces part of the responsibility for guaranteeing the security of the participating athletes against attacks planned by foreign terrorists.
In closing, I wish to offer some views on the issue of security operations and individual human rights. Of all the issues involved this one is, I believe, the most critical. I should like to refer to an action in the Court of Appeal, civil division, in the United Kingdom in March, 1977, where a lower court judgment on deportation for security reasons was reviewed.
In his judgment, Lord Denning, a justice who is highly regarded and for whom I have the utmost respect, noted, "where national security was involved the rules of natural justice were liable to be modified". That is a strong statement but one which, I think, best exemplifies the seriousness of the business of ensuring national security.
What we cannot allow is covert or secret infringements of rights such as that of privacy. I say that for the hon. member for Peace River who, I am sure, agrees with that statement. At the same time we cannot hide our heads in the sand while others exploit that right to privacy covertly to plan activities harmful to us all. The balance between the two, since the

February 17, 1978

infancy of democracy, has been a mature assessment of where collective well-being overrides individual desires. The forum for deciding where one begins and the other ends and the rules which must apply to ensure a maximization of both is, in our system, parliament. What we need, through parliament, is a thorough, non-partisan examination of what tools are needed to provide for tough, effective, and openly understood powers for Canadian security units. Everyone has to know the nature of the problem such as what we may lose as individuals, we gain as a community. But it should be clear that we cannot have it both ways.
If there is no wiretapping in Canada, do not fault the police for an inability to combat organized crime. If there are no provisions for surreptitious entry into Canada, do not fault the security service for rampant espionage. If there is no provision for selective opening of the mail, blame yourself for its usage to distribute heroin, or as a conduit for messages between terrorists.
Let us not agonize about this. Police and security powers should be, must be, only those that Canadian citizens allow. I say that, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the fact that I practised law for seven years, with only one prosecution, as a defence counsel in the criminal courts of this province. In my responsibility it is a question I plan on analysing with ever-increasing seriousness. But those thoughts which I am advancing now I fully believe ware justified. If there is no provision for those measures that are required for the implementation and the protection of national security, then we can blame no one for it but ourselves for any infringement of that national security. Police and security powers should be, as I indicated, those that are presented by parliament. We should not advance more than one drop necessary in order to get the job done. But at least recognize that there is a job to be done, Mr. Speaker, and an important one at that; one which cannot be realized without full citizen commitment and understanding.
Some members of the RCMP exercised powers which were not given to them. They broke the law. That is unacceptable and that is why we have a Royal commission of inquiry looking into the matter; a commission of inquiry requested by the opposition and appointed by this government. But the fact the RCMP used authority they did not have and that they will have to answer for doing so, does not negate the reality that they ought to have such power. Indeed, I believe that to be the case, and so does the government.
If nothing else, the controversy surrounding RCMP operations has brought home to Canadians the importance of security activity in this country. It has underscored the reality that the requisite to citizen control is citizen awareness. In that sense we are growing up. The world is, and always has been, an imperfect place. One has only to look at the opposition benches to recognize that reality, Mr. Speaker.
Canada is not isolated. We continue to be the target of many threats. That is inevitable and must be accepted. Understanding that, as we have not done before, we must accept responsibility collectively for ensuring that aspect of Canadian security. We cannot continue, as we have done, to leave the

responsibility to others to improvise and do the best they can. That is the invitation to excess and those who were involved in the excess really reflect an abdication, on all our parts, of not having faced up to the issue of national security long ago.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate which is so serious calls for something beyond simple conventional criticism. My colleague from Champlain (Mr. Matte) has been denouncing for a long time this outrageous and shocking way of dealing with changes that are necessary in this Canada that we would want to reflect the deep aspirations of its people.
The present leaders of this beautiful country did not understand a thing. They closed their eyes to see what they wanted to see. This narrow-mindedness, Mr. Speaker, can only generate tremendous difficulties. Besides seeing only what they wanted to see and hearing only what they wanted to hear they remained deaf to legitimate warnings, adequate recommendations and fair and reasonable claims. So it is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, that the government should have remained deaf to the reports it was getting on the illegal, illicit and criminal activities perpetrated by a small group of terrorists.
Those allegations made by my colleague from Champlain are serious, very serious indeed. They are based on facts and true documents which can be readily consulted. Allow me, Mr. Speaker, by referring to the official issue of the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts of November 14, 1969, to quote the extract of the testimony before that committee of the testimony before that committee of the then chairman of the Executive Committee of the City of Montreal, Mr. Lucien Saulnier, and I quote:
Mr. Chairman, and members of committee. I would like the subject to be clearly understood within its context. I will therefore read some passages that are in the document that has just been distributed to you, and which reports the observations I made, Saturday, October 11 last.
We now know that in Canada, individuals and groups are working actively to implement a plan which will carry the destruction of freedom, of our form of

February 17, 1978

democratic government and, in this plan, the people's will, as expressed in the ballot box, is excluded.
These individuals and groups are inspired and financed, in many cases, by foreign political powers related to an "international" that does not share our notion of man's fundamental liberties.
In other cases, the same ideas and the same plan of action are supported by the government of Canada through The Company of Young Canadians.
For many months now, we have made the seizure of a substantial quantity of documents which justify the preceding statement with the greatest certainty. It is enough to-day, and it is my duty to do so, to raise publicly a corner of the curtain.
The partial revelations to which I will limit myself to-day are but a small example of things I know and of which I have privately informed the Prime Minister of Canada a few times in the past year.
Mr. Speaker, please note this was on November 27, 1969. Mr. Saulnier, a sensible and responsible man, comes to Ottawa to force the federal government to act, as he himself stated, after having previously informed the Prime Minister of everything. He does not understand the government's almost reprehensible indifference. He understands all the less as the federal police force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, is actually aware of all terrorist activities going on in Quebec. Once again, I would like to restrict myself to Mr. Saulnier's statement, and 1 quote:
On the other hand, I am informed by reliable sources that the RCMP has all the information at its disposal that is in the hands of the Montreal Police Department and we are of the opinion that the Government of Canada can no longer leave the whole weight of this effort to ensure the safeguard of its democratic institutions as the sole responsibility of the Police Department of Montreal.
I suggest most respectfully to your Committee that it assure itself that the RCMP has informed the Solicitor General of Canada and the Minister of Justice of the facts of which it is aware, and if it has done so, what matters the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice have taken in this regard; and if not, why the RCMP has not reported to the ministers responsible.
Mr. Speaker, we have to be very concerned about these statements. Since the RCMP was fully aware of the illegal and criminal activities of terrorist groups, how can we believe that the Solicitor General and the entire cabinet were not also aware of them? In any case, Mr. Saulnier gave firm evidence that proves that the Prime Minister was informed of this situation well before the date of this committee meeting. Once again, Mr. Speaker, to make my point, I would like to quote further from the evidence of Mr. Saulnier. These statements can be found on page 74 of the Minutes, Proceedings and Evidence of this committee. I quote:
I must add that several months ago, the Director of the Montreal Police Department drew my attention to the nature of this information concerning
these activities, and he emphasized the aspect which involved the federal authorities. 1 actually communicated with the highest officials of the government of Canada.
Mr. Sheppard, counsel for the committee, then asked Mr. Saulnier:
When was that?
Mr. Saulnier replied:
From memory, I would say it happened from 9 to 12 months ago. 1 informed the federal authorities, namely the Prime Minister of Canada. Since I was advised that the information we had was also in the hands of the RCMP, 1 suggested that the federal authorities obtain them.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, even though this might seem incredible, the government, or at least the Prime Minister, was well aware of the conspiracy that led to October 1970 at least two years before those tragic events. I say two years at least, since my colleague for Champlain also proved that the RCMP was aware of all the activities of the FLQ since the very first outbursts of terrorism. It is difficult to imagine that the senior officers responsible for this police force thought it advisable not to inform government authorities.
Let us not be childish and believe those fairy tales. The government took full advantage of the opportunity it had to discredit an honest and democratic movement which was only arriving at Quebec emancipation and fulfilment. They would indirectly control those subversive activities. How could the infiltration of the Compagnie des Jeunes Canadiens by former FLQ members be otherwise explained? What made a police force as efficient as the RCMP unable to find and disrupt those terrorist groups for ten years? How could the fact that criminal action by the police was disclosed by the Solicitor General himself be accounted for? Mr. Speaker, I believe that like any ordinary citizen, a police officer should obey the law, all the more so because he is responsible for its enforcement. Otherwise, we would have to infer there are two kinds of police: One involved in the protection of citizens against criminals and the other committing offences under the Criminal Code while pretending to ensure national security.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that our police officers generally behave like gentlemen in their routine daily tasks and that is not always easy, 1 must admit. But, the worst part, to my mind, is that some high ranking senior officers sometimes seem to indulge in low political intrigues. This is the key to the whole thing, Mr. Speaker. This government, under the pretense of national security, attacked a nationalist party that was legitimate in Quebec as if it were a crime to aim at rebuilding Canada according to the wishes of its people. Of course, as they needed an excuse to fight a sound and legitimate movement, they had to make out it was a subversive and criminal organization.
Instead of setting upon terrorist criminals, they attacked an ideology. So, they have let circumstances and events happen when they could have been prevented of eliminated. This is a terrible action that will have to be explained sooner or later by those responsible. In conclusion, I stress once again the necessity of knowing the whole truth concerning those obscure events of October 1970. A whole population was traumatized and unfairly disparaged because of the failure of a government more interested in constitutional wrangles than in the welfare and freedom of the people. Let justice and truth prevail. Such is the purpose of that motion moved by the the hon. member for Champlain that I am pleased to support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been suggested by the hon. member who has just spoken, the plea in this motion, like the plea in the very effective speech made by the hon. member for Peace River
February 17, 1978

(Mr. Baldwin), is in these words: tell us the facts; tell us the truth.
I believe very strongly that the hon. member for Peace River was stating what needs to be said, namely, that no government can govern effectively unless it has the confidence of the House of Commons, the confidence of the people of Canada. If the credibility of this government has suffered to the point at which many people are losing faith in it and are losing faith in the governmental process, it is largely because of the secrecy, sometimes the deception, which the government insists in practicing with respect to police affairs and with respect to what goes on in the province of Quebec.
I regret very much that the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), in the speech he made a few moments ago, gave no indication that he got the message the motion was put down to convey to him and that he had no appreciation of the message which the hon. member for Peace River directed to him as well. His speech was simply a defence of past and continuing secrecy in matters of security, a defence of the demand for more rights and powers for the police, and 1 would say it showed an utter failure on his part to recognize how important it is to turn things around and move in the direction of open government.
The motion itself, of course, is drafted with reference to the events of October, 1970, which all of us remember so well. I remember in particular the decision which we in our caucus took a few hours before the matter was discussed in parliament. We knew when we decided we would have to oppose the use of the War Measures Act in that situation that, for a time at least, we would be very unpopular, not only in this House but throughout the country. And that was the way it turned out, too. But as the years have gone on, many people have come to realize that it was too heavy an instrument to use in that situation and that we were right in our opposition to the proclamation of the War Measures Act in October, 1970. Indeed, I think that one of the most statesmanlike utterances made in recent years was the comment by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) a while ago in which he commended the then leader of this party, my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), and the then deputy leader of this party, Mr. David Lewis, for the leadership they gave on that occasion.
Time has passed by and other things have happened. There were the events of 1972 and 1973, shrouded in secrecy. The hon. member for Peace River was quite right, in my view, when he said that had we known what was going on the political history of this country might have been changed sharply. In addition, Mr. Speaker, some of us think that the national unity crisis we have today has been made sharper because certain situations and forces in the province of Quebec were exacerbated by the heavy hand of the War Measures Act.
I regret very much that the speech of the Solicitor General today shows no indication of realizing the seriousness of the situation. It is all very fine to say we have a beautiful country

with less violence and less disturbance than most countries in the world, but we are suffering a traumatic crisis in terms of national unity and a good deal of that arises from the way in which the situation was handled in October, 1970. I am sorry that the Solicitor General, instead of responding to the one specific thing that is in the motion, chose to defend the way in which he and the government are running affairs.
I said that there is one specific request in the motion, and I draw it to the attention of the Solicitor General. In the opening part of his remarks he said he was sorry the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) had made no proposals and had said nothing positive. He said the hon. member had just ranted and raved about things in this country from his own point of view. Has the Solicitor General not read the motion? The key words after the usual words of preamble are these, that the House-
-therefore directs the Solicitor General to disclose in public all the facts and circumstances pertaining to the authority given to the RCMP to act as they did before, during and after the October 1970 events.
That is the request in the motion. That is what our party wanted in 1970. I remind the government opposite that several times during October and November of 1970 the then minister of justice, Mr. John Turner, promised the House that when it was all over we would be told the whole story. We are still waiting.
The hon. member for Peace River referred earlier today to the extravagant speech which was made by Mr. Jean Mar-chand when he was a minister on the other side of the House. There were some pretty strong statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as to what was going on, to the extent that many people feel today that the country was misled as to the nature of the situation. The answer to our complaints about this sort of thing back in 1970 was that when it was all over the full story would be told. Now, when there is a motion before the House asking that the full story be told, the Solicitor General does not even comment on that appeal.
The hon. member for Peace River was quite right in drawing attention to the parallel between 1970 and 1972 and 1973 in terms of events which were going on and about which we knew nothing. Secrecy is still the way this government believes it has to run things. Mr. Speaker, this is an old issue-freedom of information, open government, the basic principles of democracy. I heard the fine philosophy the Solicitor General indulged in about where you draw the line between national security and freedom, but it seems to me the government has shown by its practices that it leans the wrong way.
I cannot and do not go along with all the things the hon. member for Champlain put forward in his speech. He was talking about many things of which I have no knowledge, but in terms of the basic appeal in the motion itself, namely, that the House should call upon the government to give us the facts about the October crisis of 1970, I am glad the motion is before us. I am glad the hon. member for Peace River addressed himself to it in the way he did and I join with all who take that view in saying that I hope we may yet get out of the government that which was promised in 1970, namely, the full story.

February 17, 1978

Furthermore, let that become the principle of government. Let that become the way things are run in Canada; let the government govern not in secrecy, not by giving the police more powers but, rather, on the basis of openness of the kind which will enable the people to trust government, to trust the parliamentary process. We would be a lot better off that way than we are the way things are now being run by the government across the aisle.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are today facing a huge scrambling operation. In fact, I think that the motion before us today in the House is futile and dilatory, and it is not in a lighthearted manner that I take the floor to join the debate. I think that the incongruities uttered by the member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) have to be staunchly denounced.
Mr. Speaker, this morning the hon. member for Champlain made all sorts of insinuations, slanderous remarks and accusations, he mixed up some facts, dodged other facts and drew his own conclusions. Mr. Speaker, what is he actually seeking by presenting such a motion today? I am asking myself the following question: Why is it that a member whom I otherwise respect very much, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), associated himself with such muck raking and confusion breeding tactics? Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, objectivity is a rather scarce commodity these days. Some will say that it is even more scarce in the field of politics. It may be so, I agree. Some people look at things through a magnifying glass. They scrutinize the facts, blissfully ignoring the context of a given situation. Some look at the facts through the small end of the scope. They are so general in their remarks that they forget what is important as well as the details. But in the case of the hon. member for Champlain, Mr. Speaker, I am under the impression that he looks at the facts through a frosted glass. His vision is so blurred that you end up asking yourself what is he getting at. You can even ask yourself the following question: What does he actually want to accomplish by presenting the facts that way? Is he trying, Mr. Speaker, to resuscitate the dead? He referred to the history of Quebecers throughout the years, he stated that they are peaceful people who respect institutions, who are law abiding, who like order and he immediately jumped to the conclusion that it was impossible for insurrection to take place in our country, in our province, because of that peaceful and quiet history. Mr. Speaker, there is no causal relation between the two. I do not understand very well how he intellectually proceeds to arrive at such a conclusion. In any event, he mentioned a whole series of facts chosen at random, he tried to relate these facts in order once again to derive fallacious conclusions. Mr. Speaker, I have had a lot of difficulty following his thought and this is why I am saying that what is left of that whole issue is nothing but a blurred and unhealthy hodge-podge.
Mr. Speaker, the member for Champlain referred for instance to the Samson affair. He stated that Samson is not dead. But he did not go on with his argument. He planted doubts about the activities of officer Samson, and regarding

the orders he was supposedly complying with. This is why I say that this way of presenting facts draws dangerously close to some form of intellectual dishonesty. This is why I feel obliged today to take part in this debate, in order to try and denounce this situation as strongly as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I definitely will not endorse the contents of the Opposition motion presented today by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) on behalf of the Social Credit party. I think once again that the confusion in the terms of the motion-and I urge all hon. members to reexamine this motion-cannot but lead me to ask very serious questions first, about the facts that are stated, second, about the conclusions drawn by the member, and third, about whatever he is asking the government to do.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, what is the gist of that motion? It is the War Measures Act. I was not a member of this House in 1970 when it approved the government motion for the proclamation of war measures. The hon. member for Champlain was a member at that time. Where was he? Nowhere. I looked, Mr. Speaker, and I stand to be corrected if I am wrong, I looked for an intervention from the hon. member for Champlain when the War Measures Act was discussed in this House. 1 found none whatsoever, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, his leader was in the House and he accepted the arguments put forward at that time. He said, Mr. Speaker, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, of course the measures we intend to approve today make poor publicity for us abroad. However, we must cope with the situation. The government can rely on our support to prevent recurrence of such acts as have been perpetrated.
Mr. Speaker, when the vote was called for implementation of the War Measures Act, the Social Credit party did support the government but the hon. member for Champlain was not there. If at that time he thought there was no state of apprehended insurrection, why did he not say so? Why did he not vote against the motion at that time? Or must have realized later on that supporting the War Measures Act had been like using a steam-roller to crush an ant-hill. This is possible, and I recognize that it is questionable.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I do not see why he comes to us today, in 1978, and implies that there was no apprehended insurrection and, this is even more serious, I ask myself questions in the light of his statement that the RCMP stirred up these disorders. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, to refer to Constable Samson, to try and relate this thing to the theft of dynamite he mentioned, to try and relate both events to other unfortunate incidents which are at present being investigated by a Royal Commission-he carefully avoided saying that there was such an inquiry on this matter, but implied, and once again, it is easy to imply, that nothing would be known of the conclusions of this commission since it is in the government's pay, is merely jumping to conclusions.
It is very easy to do that, Mr. Speaker. Insinuations can be made by the dozen but, Mr. Speaker, one cannot necessarily draw conclusions from insinuations, and I am afraid that the hon. member is systematically drawing his own conclusions,
February 17, 1978

one by one, and, setting himself up as an accusator, an arbitrator and a judge he states: as the RCMP acted illegally in the past, there was no apprehended insurrection in Quebec, there were just one or two score trouble-makers and the War Measures Act was perhaps simply a tool in the hands of the government. And there, we do not know exactly what he means or what he is suggesting. Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to something more important. Let us not forget that the hon. member for Champlain takes pleasure in ambiguity, Mr. Speaker. Let us not forget that the ideas of the hon. member for Champlain on our institutions are not as clear as they ought to be, and it is his prerogative to behave in such a way. He talks about a Quebec community, a Quebec nation, but very seldom refers to our federal institutions.
Mr. Speaker, in an effort to reflect upon the RCMP, would the hon. member for Champlain not be playing another game? I do not know. Yet, having heard the remarks he made this morning, I cannot help wondering, Mr. Speaker, which is unfortunate in a debate such as this. In fact when you make gratuitous accusations, or hastily draw wrong conclusions, or make nebulous suggestions, you sow the seeds of doubt in the public's mind something which I feel is extremely dangerous, Mr. Speaker, and should be exposed.
Mr. Speaker, I referred a while ago to the War Measures Act. I was a student at the time, and I must say that I had then and still have serious reservations about the implementation of that legislation. As I was saying, in view of the way the events were described at the time, the government may very well have overreacted-something which is debatable-in its use of the judiciary.
We were not aware of this in 1970, Mr. Speaker. We heard about it later! When the Prime Minister of Canada appeared before this House and asked for support of the motion, he did state that actual events as well as the information he had received pointed out to a potential danger. That is what he claimed at that time, after reading a letter from the Quebec prime minister requesting, and I emphasize the word "requesting" federal intervention. His Honour Jean Drapeau, the Mayor of Montreal, also wrote a letter stating that, in view of the circumstances, additional forces were needed to restore order. Mr. Trudeau, who was Prime Minister at that time stated on October 16, 1970, and I am quoting from his speech:
In spite of this political climate, a handful of fanatics is enough to ...
We are not talking in terms of hundreds of people-
... a handful of fanatics to show us how fragile a democratic society can be when democracy is not prepared to stand up, and how vulnerable to blackmail a humane and tolerant people can be.
Those are the facts, Mr. Speaker. Again, the fact that there has been a few dozen convictions does not justify our jumping to conclusions after the fact-it is easy after eight years-and to say there was no apprehended insurrection, indirectly alleging at the same time that the RCMP was there to stir up trouble and speed up the passage of this measure. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but it is very difficult for me to understand the reasoning and the mental process that lies behind all this.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, in the circumstances I believe I have established clearly enough that the allegations of the hon. member for Champlain are unfounded, at least so is the inference he derived from them.
I would simply like to remind the House, Mr. Speaker, that in his long list of supposedly seditious acts by the RCMP he included the death of Michel Viger. He quoted at that point a letter published in Le Devoir of December 20, 1977. However, Mr. Speaker, he quoted only what was convenient for him to quote, and I shall now complete his quote because I think it is important for the record and for the information of all Canadians. I will simply quote the rest of that letter addressed to the hon. member for Champlain, Mr. Matte, and signed by Jean Viger:
I would therefore ask you to either elaborate and prove the basis of your allegations, or retract your statements which tarnish the memory of my brother Michel.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that I have anything else to add, this proves adequately that the accusations made by the hon. member for Champlain are groundless.
