Mr. Speaker, before I deal with the substance of or the implications arising from the motion, may I be permitted to make one or two comments, the first of which is directed to my colleague who has just spoken, the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance). He and I obviously interpret the motion or its implications in different ways, because, if I understood my colleague correctly, he found this debate very distasteful or abhorrent, though I forget his exact words.
I make no comment on his interpretation of the speech by the hon. member in whose name the motion stands, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte). Nor will I attempt to comment on his interpretation of the facts that arose during that very unhappy period of our history. However, 1 do not find this debate distasteful. I wish we were permitted the luxury of debating things which are not quite so difficult to come to grips with, and if I misinterpreted the hon. member's remarks I apologize.
That hon. member did participate in a careful examination of terror in Canada, but terror of a different kind-terror in our prisons. I think he found that, while the subject of the motion was not an easy thing to come to grips with, at least it is productive and a responsible thing to do. If I misinterpret what the hon. member said I hasten to apologize, but I got the impression he found this motion a distasteful subject to bring to the floor of the House of Commons. That was obviously a misinterpretation.
May I deal very briefly with what the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) said, or did not say. Unfortunately he would not come to grips with what I think is the issue here. I will just make one or two comments on his remarks.
Firstly, he was very disappointed that an atmosphere of partisanship had been created. For a Solicitor General to be
2990

February 17, 1978

living in a glass house such as that is difficult to understand. He has come to his present office through a very unhappy and regrettable set of circumstances which created the vacancy there. I can only presume that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in seeking to fill that vacancy, did not ask himself who was best able, through experience, for example, to deal with the present system, or who was most sensitive to the pressures and responsibilities that flow from becoming Solicitor General, or who has served the longest on the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Those were not the criteria used in the selection of a successor. The criterion was: where could the Prime Minister find a good, tough, hard-nosed debater who could stonewall and sandbag in the House of Commons? That was the criterion and that is a matter perfectly within the responsibility and judgment of the Prime Minister. That is not the criterion I would choose, but I do not deny him that right.
The present Solicitor General has dedicated himself to tough, partisan debates in this House for five and a half years. He is good at it; that has been his style and his responsibility in this House. But let us not try to mislead the House into thinking there has been a remarkable transformation on the part of the present Solicitor General, when all of a sudden overnight, or within two weeks, we see a move from what was a very tough, partisan Liberal backbencher to a completely non-partisan, sensitive and delicate Solicitor General. That is simply incomprehensible. Let us remove that part of his contribution, or lack of it, from this debate.
The other thing that the Solicitor General preoccupied himself with, for whatever reason I do not know, was the excellence, on the one hand, of the security service, which no one is debating, and, on the other, the very delicate line between civil rights and the necessity to preserve our national security. That is not an issue in this debate. Let me say to the Solicitor General, in respect of mail interception, for example, that I support in principal the legal interception of mail in certain special and specified circumstances, given adequate safeguards and when other more usual law enforcement measures are ineffective. There is no quarrel there.
It is very regrettable that the Solicitor General did not come to grips with what I believe to be the implication of the motion proposed by the hon. member for Champlain. The implication as I understand it is the continuing inability of Canadians to know the full facts and truth about a very unhappy part of Canada's history. That is the implication I understand from this particular motion.
I was not a member in October 1970 and I did not live in that part of Canada which was most directly subjected to these events. However, I share the concern of the mover, and I think of all Canadians, that we do not know and are unable to know what were the events and the facts that surrounded and led up to that very unhappy situation. I say this because the Prime Minister has set the style in the context of our times in 1978. I will come to that matter in a few minutes.
There was a time in this House when all of the facts could have come out very properly in a forum constituted for that

purpose. This was in the days following May 13, 1971 when the then minister of justice, John Turner, made this motion:
That a special joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to examine, inquire into and report upon the nature and kind of legislation required to deal with emergencies that may arise from time to time in the future by reason of lawlessness or violence in Canadian society and that endanger the existence of government or the maintenance of the peace and public order;-
The motion goes on to say that there shall be 12 members of that special committee, which will have the power to sit during the adjournment of the House, the power to report from time to time, and so on. That motion was moved on May 13, 1971, and of course it was prompted by the need to repeal the temporary Public Order Act. It was also prompted by the void that existed between, on the one hand the Criminal Code and, on the other hand, the War Measures Act, a very obvious and continuing void.
On that same day, May 13, 1971, an amendment was put by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). It read as follows:
That the motion be amended by adding at the end of the first paragraph thereof the following: "and, for better assuring the purposes of such report with respect to emergencies that endanger the existence of government, inquire into and first report upon all the circumstances anticipatory of and giving rise or purporting to have given rise to the proclamation of the War Measures Act on October 16, 1970, as well as all the circumstances thereafter following and thereto related which may have or presently or in future may endanger the existence of any government, whether federal, provincial or municipal".
There was a debate on the admissibility of that amendment. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) put it succinctly in one sentence-and I ask him to excuse me for quoting him while he is here in the House-when he said:
How in the name of heaven can a joint committee examine what it proposes to do in the future regarding emergencies of this kind unless it examines the procedures of the past?
Mr. Speaker ruled that the amendment was in order, and John Turner and his colleagues ran for cover. There is no other way to describe what happened than to say it was a simple retreat in disorder from an obvious responsibility of the government of the day. They had no idea that that amendment would be in order, and the minute it was, they went full speed in reverse. Because they did not believe that Canadians should have the right, through their elected representatives, to have a properly constituted, special committee to examine this crucial area. Therefore, not only do we not have a special committee, we have no legislation.
Five months later, the hon. member for Calgary North tried again to resurrect this government order but was turned down. Seven months later, in December of that year, the hon. member for Peace River tried to get some assurance that that particular matter would stand over into the next session, but he was turned down. Therefore, we have no legislation. To the everlasting shame of this government, we have no legislation to fill the void between the Criminal Code and the War Measures Act.
February 17, 1978

Why do we not have this legislation? Not for purposes of national security; that is absolute nonsense. This information is not being withheld for purposes of national security. It is being withheld because of the government's paranoia and passion for secrecy. They do not know what is secret any more. They have forgotten the original reason for keeping information secret because every report and every communique is presumed to be secret unless someone can prove to the contrary. The presumption is secrecy, not openness, and if you start from that point, almost everything will be secret. As I said, I will put it in the context of today. What is the context of today? Is it the peaceful and quiet Canada that the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) spoke of earlier this afternoon? It is not peaceful and quiet. We are a peaceful and quiet nation by tradition and through our heritage, but it is not peaceful and quiet in Canada today. We have just witnessed the expulsion of 13 Russian nationals. We have reports of 300 Russian and Cuban trained terrorists in our country. We have reports of the funding of terrorist activities. We have, as the Solicitor General said, the danger of foreign agents operating here or coming here to operate. We have arms smugglers. And, to use the Solicitor General's words of earlier this afternoon, we have real threats. The result is, not panic, but concern, and so it should be. But we find it so distasteful that we are not willing to come to grips with it.
In Germany they are coming to grips with it. Today's issue of the Journal contains a headline which reads "Bitter Bonn Anti-terrorist Debate". I presume that our colleagues in Germany are not relishing that debate, but they are coming to grips with it. Some members voted against a particular piece of legislation because they thought it went too far, while others thought it went not far enough; but they are coming to grips with it. We are not. We do not even have a piece of legislation in place which would fill the void I spoke of.
What has this led to? It has led to the concern I mentioned but, what is far more dangerous, it has led to cynicism. People are cynical about national security, and of all issues where we do not need or want cynicism, it is in terms of law enforcement, law and order and national security.
The Solicitor General said-I believe I quote him almost verbatim-that he deplored the motion and the speech of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) because what he was looking for, or what he wanted, was suggestions for improving the Solicitor General's ability to deal with his responsibilities and with national security matters, but that we had made no such suggestions.
I will give him one suggestion and I will give him an opportunity to stand up on a point of order and reply to it. 1 call on the Solicitor General to resurrect the Turner motion of 1971 with the amendment. He cannot possibly say that one cannot look at the events of the past to determine what legislation we will have in the future. He cannot have the McDonald commission making recommendations without investigating activities which have led to those recommendations. So I will give him that positive suggestion upon which he can act. Let him bring in the motion which Mr. Turner

brought in 1971, perhaps in more compatible terms with today's activities but certainly pursuing the same end, and from which he retreated with full force along with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the rest of the cabinet when they thought there might be some disclosure of facts leading to the necessary legislation. That is a positive suggestion, and we will support it on this side.
Let him not say this is a matter more properly to be considered by the McDonald commission. This has nothing to do with the McDonald commission. I agree with the Solicitor General that the law enforcement agencies of this country need the necessary tools and legislation to fulfil their serious responsibility. What we are talking about is, what legislation does the government have for a situation in which we would have terrorist activity with which we would have to deal quickly? There is no point hiding behind the McDonald commission when it comes to resurrecting that particular motion and the amendment to it. If the Solicitor General is serious in looking for means to aid law enforcement agencies and fellow Canadians in dealing with security matters, surely nothing is more self-evident than to put faith in members of the House to deal with the proposed legislation to counter terrorist activities once they have occurred. It is as evident today as it was in 1971 that he, as this country's senior law enforcement officer is responsible for national security, has the obligation to fill the void that existed in 1970 and which continues to exist today.
Surely that is something which cannot be shunted aside or subjected to a shroud of secrecy. Surely there cannot be a plausible argument against constituting that committee, which was a great idea, according to Mr. Turner and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in 1971, until they realized that some facts would be disclosed. I call upon the Solicitor General to bring before this House a government order constituting either a special joint committee or a committee of this House to study the events before and after the crisis of October, 1970 with a view to recommending legislation to the House of Commons and to the other place which would properly fill the void which exists now between the Criminal Code and the War Measures Act.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps it would be worthwhile to look at a few of the assertions in the motion because I have not yet heard in this debate anyone comment on the following one:
That this House deeply regrets that the government, through neglect or because of its connivance with the police, allowed the whole of Canada in general and Quebec in particular to be engulfed in a crisis ...
I think we should look at that statement carefully because it attacks the government as well as the police. The motion does not single out the Quebec Provincial Police, the RCMP, the Quebec city police or the Montreal city police. It refers to the police generally.
Although I am not a lawyer, I believe that negligence consists of doing something a prudent person would not do. I
80031 -48!4

February 17, 1978

suppose the negligence referred to by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) is the imposition of the War Measures Act. I have to assume that because 1 cannot tell from reading this motion.
The second allegation is that if the federal government was not negligent, it connived with the police to cause a crisis in Canada in general and in Quebec in particular. In other words, the government somehow contrived to bring about a situation so that it could impose the War Measures Act. I have listened to hon. members opposite make speeches on capital punishment and on other things, and I know that they are very much aware of the need for law enforcement and for strong legislation to protect law-abiding citizens. However, this motion states that the government may have connived with the police to cause a crisis.
I do not think the government allowed a crisis to come about with its knowledge. I suspect that a group of terrorists, the FLQ, perpetrated acts of terrorism such as bombings and kidnappings without the by-your-leave of the federal government. I suspect that these things were done at murky levels, if I may use that term. Certainly these things were not done in the light of day. The government of Canada was not able to prevent that situation because it cannot grab people off the street for things they think or plan. There has to be concrete proof that people are breaking the law.
The motion alleges that if there was not negligence, the federal government connived with the police so that it could create a situation in which it could bring in the War Measures Act. I do not think that is what happened. I think that 50, 100 or perhaps 200 people-I am not aware of the number, and I understand it was not very large-brought the situation about. We have seen what can happen when one or two terrorists hijack an aircraft, kidnap a wealthy industrialist or do a variety of things. One or two people, let alone 100 or 200, can cause panic.
With hindsight we wonder whether the government overreacted to the situation or, as some people might suggest, did not go far enough. I know that the New Democratic Party opposed the War Measures Act, but it also voted as a group against the retention of capital punishment. The philosophy of the NDP is different from mine. I have always believed that those who break the law, whether they be terrorists or premeditated murderers, should be dealt with very severely. The NDP does not believe that, and that is its prerogative.
I was not a member of this House in 1970, but 1 was a resident of this country, and although I lived in B.C., far from Quebec, I felt that whatever affects one province or area affects the whole country. A sore thumb or hand affects the whole body. In 1970 the people of Canada felt that acts of terrorism such as kidnappings, bombings and political assassination were foreign to our country and that the government should proceed with despatch to ensure that acts of that nature did not spread. I respect the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but I wonder what guarantees he could have given in 1970, if strong measures were not taken or if a strong federal presence was not apparent, that the crisis would
not have spread. If it is perceived that in a crisis prompt action is forthcoming, that tends to stop the spread of that crisis. If terrorists see that their fellows are dealt with effectively, does this not indicate to sympathizers that it would not be in their best interests to become involved? The very fact that strong action was taken perhaps prevented the terrorist activities of others.

speechtext:
I cannot give figures any better than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as to what effect the War Measures Act had on the situation. However, I perceive that most Canadians, whether they be in British Columbia or Newfoundland, believe that those who transgress the laws of the country should be dealt with effectively, especially in a situation in which there is a group dedicated to the violent overthrow of the government. Most people feel that groups like that should be dealt with firmly and effectively. I suspect the people of Canada still feel that way not only about the FLQ in 1970 but about the whole question of preserving and maintaining our society for law-abiding citizens. Most people do not think there should be special concessions or exemptions for people who may be involved in criminal activities, whether that be the sale of heroin or any of the activities that we know exist in Canada through the efforts of organized crime.
I realize many people in this House and across the country may say that we must have due process of law, and I agree with that. But surely it should be the duty of government to protect our law-abiding citizens above those who transgress against the law. Surely the people of Canada expect this House to protect their interests. I know members would certainly protect the interests of law-abiding people above those who transgress against the law.
There is some question about whether a crisis existed in 1970.1 suggest that bombing, rioting, kidnapping and political assassination constitute a crisis and that the government of Canada not only has the right but the duty to respond to that crisis. If that is not the case them I am willing to listen to argument, but I suggest that a crisis did exist.
To explore in hindsight the question of how much pressure should be applied is fruitless. I suspect the only one who comes out ahead in this argument is a premier of a certain province very close to us.
I was very surprised to see members from the province of Quebec stand up and criticize the police and government and at the same time have the backing of the two opposition parties. I realize that in a democracy one can say whatever one wishes, but going strictly on the politics of this I do not think it has hurt the Liberal party. According to statements made in this debate it is the Liberal party that turns out to be the law and order party of Canada, not the Conservatives.
We have provided some more ammunition for the press of Quebec to use tomorrow and on Monday. The member from

February 17, 1978

this side who spoke ahead of me asked what the point was of bringing this motion forward at this particular time. Of course, the opposition parties thought it was a good time to hit the Liberal government, forgetting about national unity and the Quebec newspapers; just get the Liberals because an election is coming. Are they more interested in obtaining power than in keeping this country together? From some of the things that was said it seems that certain people are more interested in political gain than in keeping the country together. That is why I applaud the remarks of the hon. member who spoke before me. He was the first to put this motion in its proper context, the political one. It will give Mr. Levesque ammunition and will hurt the federalist cause in Quebec.
I say that in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, and wish to dissociate myself from the remarks of those who attacked both the federal government and the police force. This gives Mr. Levesque another free ticket. Why not just send money to him for his campaign to separate from Canada? He is grabbing at every speech made regarding the police and the events of 1970 and claiming that is what he is saying in the province of Quebec, that people cannot trust the police so they have to get out of confederation.
This position is aided and abetted by members of the opposition. Perhaps we will get down to the context in which we should be debating this rather than dealing with points of order about what should have been done in a legalistic sense eight years ago.
Mr. Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to participate in this debate. I strongly support the remarks of my colleague the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance).

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) referred to an excerpt from the speech I made in this House on October 27, 1977, when I repeated parts of a speech I had made previously about the need to reconsider the War Measures Act and the advisability of making substantial amendments with a view to ensuring that in this country civic and political liberties be always guaranteed by the judicial institutions, whatever the political context in which they are exercised.
The hon. member for Peace River read an extract from my speech. He also referred to an answer given by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) in his press conference which followed the debate, and it is following that answer from the Prime Minister that 1 wrote to the hon. member for Peace River on November 22, 1977, and also to the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), asking them what was their party's position on the need to reconsider the advisability of leaving the War Measures Act as is in our statutes to face emergency situations such as we had experienced in 1970.
The leader of the New Democratic Party answered me on January 23, 1978. Since that letter has not yet been made public, I will take the liberty, with the permission of the hon. member for Winnipeg-North-Centre (Mr. Knowles) of reading it to you, because in my opinion it is crucial to today's

debate. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby wrote as follows: In answer to your letter of November 22, 1977, I should like to restate the position that the New Democratic Party has always taken towards the War Measures Act, a position which has not changed since 1970. If one refers to the debates which took place in this House following the implementation of the War Measures Act, it is quite obvious that the NDP strongly advocated that this act be amended or repealed.
We think that the War Measures Act could lead to an abuse of parliamentary powers, a derogation of the Constitution of Canada and the violation of rights and freedoms Canadians enjoy. In fact, Mr. Lewis, the former leader of the New Democratic Party, opposed the motion to set up a parliamentary committee, the main purpose of which would have been the drafting of a special legislation similar to the War Measures Act. In the remarks he made in this House, as reported in Hansard on May 13, 1971, on page 5795, Mr. Lewis made it clear that, in his opinion, special legislation was not an answer to urgent situations. The New Democratic Party always maintained that the government should have the courage to introduce a bill in this House. We did not see the need for a special legislation but we were in favour of amending or repealing the present act. The motion introduced in the House in 1971 said that a special act was needed and therefore did not provide for a prior consideration of its need nor mention human rights and liberties.
Although we felt that the provisions of the Criminal code allow an effective intervention in urgent cases, we introduced amendments to replace the War Measures Act. As you will undoubtedly remember, Mr. Douglas tabled in October 1970 a bill which would have forced the government to inform the country of the circumstances that call for the application of the War Measures Act. It suggested that these special powers granted under the act should be limited to the right, first, of searching without warrant, second, of making arrests without warrants if there are valid grounds to suspect that a person is participating in the apprehended insurrection and, finally, to detain a person without charges being laid for a maximum of seven days. The proposals also contained other important aspects, such as the protection of several liberties by means of the right to consult with a lawyer and the safeguard of the rights granted under the act. The New Democratic Party did not depart from that position taken in the early 70s.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) did not answer in writing the letter I sent him on November 22, nor for that matter the letter I sent him on January 19, 1978 as a follow-up to the previous letter, asking him to define the position of his party, and perhaps alos his, on the proposed amendment or repeal of the War Measures Act. He rose that afternoon and I note the answer he gave. It will be found, in Hansard and it will certainly be useful during the debate that that will take place on that matter, for that debate will at least give us an opportunity to know clearly and precisely the position of the two main opposition parties as far as the

February 17, 1978

advisability of amending or modifying the War Measures Act is concerned.
The need, Mr. Speaker, to further discuss that matter appears more obvious following the comments made by the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) in an interview with the CTV private television network at the end of 1977. Indeed the Prime Minister gave hypothetical answers to hypothetical questions. But his answers did illustrate the importance of eliminating from our statutes the causes of potential abuse of power. Of course several elements relating to the October crisis of 1970 remain difficult to understand. It seems that we get more and more information. Last January we had the opportunity to read a letter from two exiled FLQ members who, through a Montreal daily newspaper, informed us about their new views relating to the events that occurred in October 1970.
Mr. Speaker, it still remains that even if we set up a royal commission, as long as the main actors of the events of October 1970 are not allowed to appear, here in Canada before a royal commission or before a regular court to give evidence of those events, of what they did at that time and of their responsibility in connection with those events all the debates that we might have to discuss what happened and to judge people who directly or indirectly were involved in those events will always remain partial answers.
However, we have gained something from these events. Surprisingly enough, Mr. Speaker, what we have gained can be found in the legislation which has been passed by Parliament since 1970. I am referring to the concept of national security. Until the events of October 1970, national security had never been a great concern for Canadians. Of course, we had the Mackenzie Commission who had been set up a few years earlier to investigate all the implications of national security in federal agencies and especially of Canadian commitments to some foreign countries, but several of the recommendations made in this report were not implemented.
Several members mentioned a recommendation concerning the opening of mail, which emphasized the need for the government to amend certain legislation, such as the Post Office Act and the Criminal Code of Canada. So the year 1970 saw the birth of the concept of national security. This concept is rather strange and very vague. It is hard to defined and is fairly wide encompassing. In fact, it was devised by modern democracies. This is a concept that we are attempting to define through legislation to fight what is now called revolutionary warfare or urban guerillas-and countries like the Federal German Republic are now facing much more crucial situations than we had in Canada in 1970. Attempts to define this concept through legislation have always been cautious. When it is mentioned in Canadian statutes it is always in passing without complete definition. For a better understanding of the term, it is necessary to refer to the authors or to the doctrine that initiated the concept of national security.
The most recent and commendable work on this subject is, in my opinion, Joseph Comblin's "Ideology of National Security". The Solicitor General of Canada should certainly read

this work which gives the history of this concept in the legislation of some countries over the last 30 years. Comblin defines national security as follows, and I quote from page 41 of his work:
National security is the authority given to the nation by the state to impose its objectives on all opposing forces. Naturally, such an authority is powerful. It is therefore the power of government able to counter all opposing forces and to ensure that national objectives prevail.
The counsel of the Solicitor General of Canada was in the gallery earlier this afternoon. He had the opportunity to define the national security concept in his plea before the Court of Appeal in January in a procedure to invalidate or dispute the terms of reference of the Keable Commission in Montreal. He defined the national security concept as the protection of the state and the territory. I consider that definition incomplete because it does not take into account the essential purpose of national security. The purpose of national security is not to protect the state or the territory first. It is to protect the individual and collective freedom of citizens.
It may seem like a semantic emphasis, but I believe it implies a notion completely different from that of a definition oriented towards the territory or the state. In fact, if one refers to the Canadian laws passed since 1970 concerning national security, one realizes that each time this concept is invoked, the judicial protection or the control and review capacity of the courts yield to the absolute discretion given to those responsible for national security to appreciate its extent and content. For instance, In the Federal Court Act, section 41 refers to national security and removes from the review and control power of the Federal Court any dispute about the content of a document allegedly concerning national security. Also the legislation we have passed in the previous sesion to create the Human Rights Commission and to protect privacy contained a similar provision, the result of which was to remove any document concerning national security in which an individual might be interested, from the protection of the Privacy Commissioner.
We have also passed an immigration bill by which the courts have no longer jurisdiction over the request of any person residing in Canada who wishes to acquire citizenship, but who is prevented from doing so on grounds of national security, and also deprived of any right of appeal. There is also before the House a bill respecting telecommunications in Canada which also deals with national security. In this case once again, the protection granted by the CRTC disappears entirely. There is also before the House a bill that has already been read the first time which will allow the opening of mail. Again, the protection granted by the courts in the first part of the legislation disappears completely when national security is invoked.
Mr. Speaker, I think these reminders are eloquent because we realize that over the past eight years the concept of national security has been constantly recurring in the Canadian statutes and almost constantly taken outside the purview of the courts. This is disquieting. Indeed when the 1970 public order bill was enacted, a provision in that legislation clearly pointed to the implications of national security when the arm of the state uses it. This is section 12, and I quote:
February 17, 1978

It is hereby declared that this Act shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights.
This means that despite any constitutional safeguards for the most essential freedoms and liberties, national security comes before anything else, even the constitution. This, Mr. Speaker, is a very significant feature. Because other countries where internal and external security was endangered to a much greater degree than was Canada's, these countries had to face situations that were no less difficult and implied more control operations than the RCMP had to perform here.
The United States of America had to review completely over the last three years the way civil freedoms and liberties in the American constitution are protected. A number of Senate committees worked on this and I would simply refer to the Senate committee meetings of October 21, 22 and 24, 1975 on the opening of the mail. These Senate meetings finally led to an executive order that was made public by President Carter on January 26, 1978. According to the press conference that followed, it is reported in the newspaper Le Figaro, on page 10, of Monday January 29, 1978, that:
President Carter has undertaken to follow it up with a legislation in Congress.
It may be interesting to refer to the contents of the American government commitment in matters of national security. 1 read from section 2-201 of the executive order. It discusses at length, the concept of national security at a time when the House must discuss two pieces of legislation dealing with the same subjects and a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate are discussing a green book tabled by the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) on freedom of information and which also refers, in the exceptions of course, to national security. So I quote part of the executive order which very clearly shows that our American neighbours have extended this concept we sanction in our courts.
The activities described in Sections ... shall be undertaken only as permitted by this order and by procedures established by the head of the agency concerned and approved by the Attorney General. Those procedures shall protect constitutional rights and privacy, ensure that information is gathered by the least intrusive means possible, and limit use of such information to lawful governmental purposes.
Activities described in Sections ... for which a warrant would be required if undertaken for law enforcement rather than intelligence purposes shall not be undertaken against a United States person without a judicial warrant, unless the President has authorized the type of activity involved and the Attorney General has both approved the particular activity and determined that there is probable cause to believe that the United States person is an agent of a foreign power.
[ Translation]
And, in the list of activities governed by the issue of a judicial warrant, we find in section 2-205 Mail Surveillance, which I quote:

No agency within the Intelligence Community shall open mail or examine envelopes in United States postal channels, except in accordance with applicable statutes and regulations. No agency within the Intelligence Community shall open mail of a United States person abroad except as permitted by procedures established pursuant to Section 2-201.



That Executive Order of President Carter is very complete; not only does it make the jurisdiction of the court conditional upon the issue of a warrant for opening mail, but it also governs all spying activities on the part of American citizens provided those citizens are not suspected of being foreign agents.
Mr. Speaker, therefore the debate we are now having today can give rise to a whole lot of questions about which we may not have all the required information. I mentioned, a while ago, speaking about the October events, the fact that the main protagonists of that crisis are not in Canada. Still, this is not a reason for the Canadian democracy not to question the worst legacy left us, that event namely a concept of national security that does not come under the jurisdiction of our Canadian courts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention to participate in this debate today, but the overstatements made by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) regarding the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have prompted me to say a few words. The slanderous remarks and above all the absurdities professed by the member for Champlain certainly do not meet with the approval of the members of his own party because one can see in this House that three quarters or even perhaps 90 per cent of his colleagues from the Social Credit Party of Canada have decided not to be present in the House during this debate. The hon. member for Champlain is undoubtedly aware that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has been operating in the interest of all the citizens of Canada for a period of over 100 years. This security force which is unsurpassed throughout the world has been going through difficult times in recent months.
Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether the hon. member for Champlain and some other members of this House realize that one of the first steps to be taken by a movement which wants to sabotage or destroy a country is to undermine the credibility of the security forces of that country. I am now asking myself why the hon. member allows himself to play that game? Some two weeks ago, Mr. Louis Laberge lashed at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and behaved as some kind of anarchist. It is not the first time that this man speaks like an anarchist, but his statements reinforce my conviction that we are now witnessing a deliberate and organized effort on the part of separatist elements to denigrate and damage, by all possible means, the image and the credibility of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We have in Canada, as I said earlier, one of the best security forces in the world.

When the NDP had an opportunity to take part in this debate today, no one in that party took the trouble to at least dissociate themselves from the wild exaggerations which one of their political colleagues, Louis Laberge, made a couple of weeks ago with regard to the RCMP.
I entered the debate today because, frankly, I feel that the campaign of vilification directed at the RCMP has reached

February 17, 1978

such a level, in my province at least, that one is obliged to come to the conclusion that it is nothing less than a deliberately orchestrated campaign by pro-separatist elements to destroy the effectiveness of the RCMP within the province of Quebec.
What I find amazing and sickening is the willingness of both the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the leader of the New Democratic Party to lend themselves to this game. Over the years the RCMP have served Canada well. There is no question about the fact that they are the best security force that any country in the world is fortunate to have.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: Speak the truth.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
That is the truth, and members of the opposition know it. The RCMP has been under attack for the last number of months in connection with things that happened in the province of Quebec in the course of a long history of security activities. These activities are now being brought within a more modern framework which will allow police work to be under more adequate civilian control.
The government has announced its intention to proceed in this direction. I think people have the common-sense to realize that any government of Canada would move in such a direction following reports of the kind which have come to light. We are moving toward a framework which will allow the security forces to protect the country from both internal and external threats within a completely legal set of rules. This process has been proceeding, though I must say it has been interrupted by political activity of various kinds in the last few months.

I would like to read or at least draw the attention of the Elouse to what the Quebec minister of Justice, Mr. Bedard, said in January 1977, long before the setting up of the Keable Commission. At that point, he questioned the presence of the RCMP in Quebec. Lie also questioned the necessity of maintaining a federal police force in the province. It has since then become obvious that the expulsion of the RCMP from Quebec is one of the objectives of the government in power in Quebec. It is with this objective in mind that the Keable Commission was set up. I have nothing to say against the Keable Commission because I think that Mr. Keable has done an excellent job of conducting this enquiry. He did what he had to do. He did his job with honor. But the objective which was pursued when the Commission was established was a political one, and that has to be said because it is the truth.

I want to respond to two or three things which have been said today about RCMP activities during the period the War Measures Act was used in 1970. I had the opportunity to vote for the War Measures Act at the time. I certainly did so with the conviction that it was the right thing to do, as did so many other members, and 87 per cent of the Canadian people also felt it was the right thing to do. We now hear a different opinion from some agonizers who think it was a mistake. I still
think it was the right decision taken at the right time. Of course, if we had known then everything we know now we might not have used a tank to crush a fly. But at that time we did not have information allowing us to make any decision other than the one we took.
At that time the criticism was not that the RCMP were sticking their noses into everyone's business in Quebec or that they were infiltrating Quebec organizations. The accusation was that the RCMP had not infiltrated to a sufficient extent. Now the force is under fire because it took the lesson of 1970 seriously. Members of the force infiltrated and in doing so they committed certain irregularities which were not covered by any framework of rules. We are now establishing a framework which will allow the RCMP to be covered legally in the future if they are called on to attack an internal security problem.
I am speaking heatedly about this matter because I believe all this anti-RCMP propaganda we have heard in the last few months is having a bad effect on the ability of the force to protect Canadians. The force has been under the gun for several months now. It is uncertain about what it can do and what it cannot do and its members would be less than human if their work was not affected. I am sure these attacks have had a bad effect on the ability of the RCMP to protect Canadians from external or internal threats.
There are some who pretend that the situation in Quebec in 1970 did not require strong action. I take a different view, and in support of that view I would draw the attention of the House to the experience of an acquaintance of mine who was for some reason or other making a survey of a town in the Province of Quebec during the week prior to the War Measures Act being proclaimed. He told me that normally, while engaged on this work, he would find the doors of the houses unlocked, but in that particular week every single door was locked or barred. This showed what the sentiments of the people in the Montreal region were. They were highly alarmed.
I am confident that had the government not moved when it did and as strongly as it did we would have found ourselves in a state of civil disorder. Incidents would have occurred provoking actions and counter-actions. We would have been in a terrible mess in Montreal had it not been for the firm action taken by the federal government. Those who pretend that somehow we could have avoided taking such a decisive step do not have any alternative to suggest.
It is true, more people were arrested than need to have been arrested. That is very unfortunate.

However, I should remind the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) that the RCMP lists were not the ones used for arresting these people, but rather those in the hands of the Provincial Police which proceeded with most of the arrests. The RCMP was no doubt there on some occasions, but the lists drawn up by the Provincial Police were used. I regret that too many people were arrested but it must be pointed that those who were arrested, illegally as it was learned afterwards,

February 17, 1978

receive at least a partial financial indemnity for their unfounded arrest.
In conclusion, I reiterate my personal confidence in the RCMP. This force is going to serve Canada in the future as well as it has in the past. The government will establish the legal framework which will allow it to work effectively and within the discipline required by modern society. We must have total civilian control over the activities as well as total political knowledge of what goes on. This is the government's objective. It will be achieved without the campaign of vilification the opposition parties have lent themselves to.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I did not have some respect for the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson), I would not bother answering him in the debate today. In fact, I did not intend to enter into it. The hon. member made some considerable misrepresentations in his speech relating to a very important aspect of history.
The motion before the House threshes an awful lot of old straw. He referred to our history in the 1970s. Perhaps those of us who live through this era are not the best judges. He missed the point of the motion and should be brought back to it. The motion is not with respect to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is with respect to the Government of Canada. In part the motion reads as follows:
That this House deeply regrets that the government...
It is deeply regretted that the government of Canada connived. That is the issue of the motion. I realize the hon. member is warmed up and heated. Sometimes when that is the case, an hon. member says things in the House and elsewhere which, upon reflection, he realizes should not have been said. The gist of the motion is simple. After the part about the connivance of the government, the motion directs the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais)-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: With the police force.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
I hear the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) referring to the police force. The motion directs the Solicitor General to "disclose in public all the facts". If an hon. member opposes the motion with respect to the disclosure of facts, he must be holding himself back for one of two reasons. Either he has a suspicion that the government conducted itself improperly, or there is some doubt in that person's mind as to the position of the RCMP. If the government had done nothing improper, the facts would sustain it.
I have no doubt about the work of the RCMP in 1970. I was not a member of parliament at that time, but I am sure the force acted with respect to the question of national security as directed by the government of the day. It the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has that doubt, he should express it.
I was concerned with what the hon. member for Laprairie said when he indicated that the hon. Leader of the Opposition

(Mr. Clark) attacked the RCMP. I ask him to check the record in that regard. That is factually wrong. The Leader of the Opposition said that what has been neglected, throughout this entire matter involving the security forces of Canada, is the question of ministerial responsibility. It is important to mention that in the dying moments of this debate. The doctrine of ministerial responsibility means that a minister is answerable in the House of Commons for whatever an agency does, whether the action was right or wrong. It is not proper for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), or any other minister, to indicate that he does not know what the security service or any other agency of government is doing when purportedly carrying out its duties imposed by statute. That is not the doctrine of ministerial responsibility under the British parliamentary system. That is the doctrine of ministerial ignorance. Perhaps that applies in the congressional system where there is no such thing as ministerial responsibility, but it does not apply here.
Members are hamstrung with respect to questioning ministers of the Crown in the House respecting their former responsibilities when they were ministers or when they were solicitors general of Canada respectively. The actions of the present Solicitor General, who moved to that post from that of postmaster general, do not help the situation. The Speaker of the House of Commons indicated the other day that the present Solicitor General is on probation with respect to the manner in which he exercises his ministerial responsibility.
The guts of the motion is not an attack on the RCMP. It is dangerous for hon. members to indulge in this kind of wayward chicanery. It is a demand for information. The demand has been made elsewhere than the House of Commons. The demand is: what happened in 1970? If there was disclosure, perhaps we would not have to fear the involvement of the RCMP, as was suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. In fact, he appeared not to direct himself to the motion, but rather skirted around it.
1 hope no member believes that the security services should not be responsible to someone who, in turn, is responsible to the House of Commons. I hope no one in this Chamber takes the view that it is inappropriate for the security services to be in the hands of the RCMP. I do not share that view. That is where it should be.
Somewhere along the line a shadow agency was established called the security and intelligence advisory group, or some such name. Its lines of communication and responsibilities were not clear by tradition or practice. Someone used to call them "Goyer's gumshoes". Those things ought not to be left hanging with no communication to either the head of the government or a minister of the Crown, and that is the problem here. The whole basis of accountability in respect of a ministry and in respect of this activity has been damaged as a result. The RCMP in the minds of some people in the public, not mine, is carrying the can for what I think is wilful maladministration and misdirection on the part of the government of Canada. That situation now is being remedied, I think, and I hope this continues.

February 17, 1978

The hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) then dealt with the Keable inquiry. He said it was set up as a political inquiry-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: With political objectives.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
Yes, with political objectives as the hon. member has corrected me, and I agree with him that this is exactly the purpose for which it was set up. The interesting thing is, and if my friend will check Hansard he will discover this, that at the time it was set up the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) expressed concern to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about the inquiry. The response by the Prime Minister was that it was a great thing, but that was only because it was convenient to him. He said it was appropriate for the administration of criminal justice in the province. Then, of course, when the Keable inquiry, unfettered in any way by anything at all, began to move in, because it was, and is, a political inquiry with political objectives the Prime Minister and the then solicitor general changed their tune, and we had four separate actions commenced to withhold information from the inquiry. That is the situation.
What did the government do? Certainly members of the opposition asked for the appointment of a royal commission, and I was one of them. If your Honour checks the record, you will see that this was a much different royal commission from the one that was set up, now known as the McDonald commission. I do not have the references with me but I invite hon. members to check on the kind of commission we asked to be set up. It was a commission to be established by the Chief Justice of Canada, not the government of the day. I want the record to be quite clear. The government chose not to do that. It wanted to set up its own commission which is the commission now set up under Mr. Justice McDonald. I do not know the man, but the commission is now being accused of being a little slow and not very comprehensive.
What happened to the RCMP before that commission? As the commission moves slowly day after day after day, the evidence is coming out in little bits and pieces, and every day's operation of that commission is damaging to the reputation of the RCMP. Mr. Speaker, just read your paper this morning in that regard.
That might not have happened, because I have great faith in Chief Justice Laskin. I think from him there would have been some terms of reference and conditions that would have meant at least speed, not the slow, meandering pace that is beginning to shake the confidence of the people of Canada, and certainly mine, in the McDonald commission.
When I look back and consider the subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in respect to penitentiaries, and how members on all sides of the House, in dealing with that report, moved with swiftness, honesty and complete impartiality in examining that matter of urgent and pressing moment, I am convinced it would have been best if

that committee or a subcommittee had moved in this direction. That committee would have examined this matter more swiftly and honestly here in the House of Commons than anywhere outside, and with perhaps less damage to the RCMP.
I know there is a place for royal commissions, commissions of inquiry and a whole host of things, but what has happened in Canada is that we are knee-deep in commissions and task forces. Whenever there is a problem or something a bit ticklish in this country we sweep it under the rug and appoint a royal commission or task force. I really think, on reflection, that members of this House of Commons on all sides are just as capable-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: Of being impartial?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: Yes, of being impartial, that is true. The committee on penitentiaries is proof of that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: How many committees are there like that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess I have a much higher regard for my colleagues on all sides of the House of Commons than does the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson). We are not utilizing this House to the fullest extent. This House is accountable to the people of Canada in a way that no royal commission is. I really think we made a mistake in respect of this matter. The hon. member for Laprairie is right regarding the objectives, but the Prime Minister cannot have it both ways. The Prime Minister found it convenient to answer a question one day by saying the commission was doing its job; but when it was convenient to change that he said it was a dreadful thing and brought lawsuits against its operations. Surely that is inconsistent.
I look upon this motion as directing the House of Commons to ask for the facts. The government should not refuse that from its own point of view. I believe the RCMP, in respect of the part it played in 1970, would be prepared to stand or fall on the facts, and I am prepared to bet it would stand. We ought to consider very carefully the objectives and what we in the House of Commons can do in respect of agencies. No minister of the Crown, and not even the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, as blind an apologist for the government as he is-and I say that with respect because he supports the government-should allow the government to hide behind ministerial ignorance of situations in place of the doctrine of ministerial responsibility which has served the country and parliament well. As long as we have a parliamentary system then certainly a burden falls on ministers and the Prime Minister, and no one can deny that. This has been the issue over the course of this situation in this parliament.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. It was not my intention to participate in this debate until I listened to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and felt there were some situations and some information that ought to be set straight, particularly regarding his interpretation of what the Prime
February 17, 1978

Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said about ministerial responsibility. The Prime Minister has never said or implied that ministers are not responsible for their departments. He has said, and I paraphrase him, that solicitors general, who are responsible for the RCMP, should not actively be involved in the day-today activities of that force.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: "Have a right not to know", is what he said.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
I think that that is a perfectly defensible statement. The RCMP is involved in many investigations and on occasion they have had to investigate people who are connected with, or are even members of, this chamber or who are friends of the government of the day. For the solicitor general of the day to be involved in those kinds of investigations would be dangerous and tantamount to political interference with the investigation of suspected or real criminal activity. I do not see how the opposition can fail to accept that kind of argument.
The other point I want to refer to very briefly is the point which the hon. member made with regard to the McDonald and Keable commissions. With regard to the Keable commission, he has chastised the government for not giving to that commission all the information it requested on its "fishing trip" for the separatists in Quebec. I do not think the government should have to do that. I do not think the Keable inquiry should have more power than the government that established it. The hon. member cannot pretend that the government of Canada is thwarting the effort of the Keable inquiry by refusing to give it authority which it does not have under the constitution of Canada.
The other implication in the hon. member's remarks was that the McDonald commission was set up simply as a cover to get the solicitor general off the hook.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext: I did not say that. I really did not say that, even by implication.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-RCMP ACTIVITIES CONCERNING 1970 OCTOBER CRISIS
speechtext:
That is the way
I understood the hon. member's remarks. However, 1 am prepared to accept his denial of that implication and I am glad he made that denial.
In the course of his remarks he referred to the setting up of a commission of inquiry by the Chief Justice. That seems to me to be a rather unusual suggestion. I do not pretend to be an expert on the Inquiries Act, but I cannot recall any incident of an inquiry being launched under the authority of the Chief Justice of Canada. I can just imagine the cries that would have come from the opposition if the government had followed such a course and asked Chief Justice Laskin to do that which the hon. member has suggested. The opposition would have cried out again that the government was afraid to take the responsibility for such a commission and had sloughed off their ministerial responsibility to the Chief Justice of Canada. Again I say they cannot have it both ways.
Privilege-Mr. D. W. Munro
Again the hon. member might not have been imputing motives to the commission, but I think he was very careless in his choice of words, to say the very least, when he said that a committee of the House would have proceeded with honesty, impartiality, and speed. It seems to me that the implication there is that the McDonald commission is not proceeding in that manner. I do not think it should be left to the public to infer from the hon. member's remarks that the McDonald commission is proceeding with deliberate slough, without impartiality or without honesty. I hope that is not what the hon. member was implying.

subsubtopic: MR. MUNRO (ESQUIMALT-SAANICH)-MINISTERIAL ANNOUNCEMENTS MADE OUTSIDE PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a question of privilege. After the question period a question of privilege was raised arising out of an answer given by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Guay) in reply to a question put to him by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke). The matter at issue was the manner in which an announcement was being made in Vancouver but which should have been made in the House respecting a Tariff Board ruling on wide flange steel beams entering Canada, a matter raised earlier in the House by, among others, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen), the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) and the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle).
It is my understanding that during his press conference in Vancouver today to announce the government's decision on this matter, the government spokesman, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford)-who just by chance, happens to be the member for Vancouver Centre-added that, according to his belief, a parallel announcement was to be made simultaneously in the House.
We all know that is just not the way things happened. Worse than that, we all know that we were denied this information in the House today.
Therefore, on my own behalf and on behalf of my party I want to reserve the right to return to this question of privilege on Monday once all the facts are before us. Because here is an outstanding example of the contempt shown to the House and its members by this government, not the first such incident but one which illustrates more than most the fact that power can corrupt absolutely.

frustration as well as that of any member of the opposition when a minister decides he will go to a province or location which is affected by an announcement he will make.
